title: How Sneezing Works
summary: Josh Clark and Chuck Bryant explore sneezing: the term "sternutation," why the nose's narrow passages and cilia and mast cells trigger the reflex, the afferent and efferent phases and the sneezing center in the lateral medulla (confirmed by a fisherman's lesion case), the muscles and speed involved, the eyes-popping myth, and the many causes of sneezing (rhinitis types, drugs, aging, photic sneezing, plucking hairs, arousal-induced sneezing). They cover the rare intractable sneezing record of Donna Griffiths, the sneeze-droplet spread study and COVID-era precautions, cultural blessings and superstitions, and debunk myths such as the heart stopping and sneezing preventing pregnancy. The episode closes with a listener mail about Atlanta, Texas.

segments.title: Book preorder promo
segments.summary: Hosts promote the upcoming Stuff You Should Know book and ask listeners to preorder.

segments.title: Opening banter and sternutation
segments.summary: Hosts open the show and introduce the word 'sternutation' as a clinical term for sneezing, noting its 1576 origin and related words.

segments.title: Sneezing as the body's bouncer
segments.summary: The hosts describe sneezing as an efficient reflex that expels irritants from the nose, noting that mammals sneeze and discussing dogs' reverse sneezes.

segments.title: Nasal filtration and the sneeze trigger
segments.summary: Narrow nasal passages create turbulence that pushes particles to the sides, where cilia and mast cells react, releasing histamines and sending signals to the brain. The afferent and efferent phases and the trigeminal and olfactory nerves are described.

segments.title: Muscles, force, and eyes-open myth
segments.summary: The hosts describe the whole-body muscle involvement and high-speed expulsion of air, with speeds up to about 100 miles per hour, and debunk the idea that eyes pop out when sneezing with eyes open.

segments.title: Sneezing center discovery and fisherman case
segments.summary: The sneezing center in the lateral medulla was theorized from cat studies and confirmed around 2005 by a case of a fisherman with a lesion who could not sneeze on one side after a violent sneezing fit; capsaicin tests were used.

segments.title: Causes of sneezing: rhinitis and drugs
segments.summary: Common causes of sneezing are rhinitis (allergies, colds), with other types including occupational, hormonal, drug-induced, and age-related (geriatric) rhinitis. Smoking-factory and hormone examples are mentioned.

segments.title: Photic sneezing and sneeze patterns
segments.summary: Photic sneezing is triggered by bright light, possibly due to crossover between the pupillary light reflex and sneeze reflex, and may be inherited as an autosomal dominant trait. The hosts discuss sneezing in threes and possible evolutionary reasons for the reflex in babies.

segments.title: Other triggers: hair plucking, arousal, snatiation, and intractable sneezing
segments.summary: Other triggers include plucking hairs, sexual arousal or orgasm (with a dubious explanation), and snatiation from overeating in four families. Intractable psychogenic sneezing, mostly in adolescent girls, is covered, including Donna Griffiths' record 977-day sneezing fit from 1981 to 1983.
